## Overview

In this notebook, I outline the formalization for each of the models
used in our replication of the experimental paradigm introduced in
@jern2014. All models were built in R [@R2025], following the approaches
outlined in @lee_bayesian_2014 and @frank2025experimentology.

## Model 1: Normative Model

### Formalization

Let $D \in \{L_1, L_2, Y_1, Y_2\}$ represent the patient's true disease,
$C \in \{\text{Allozedic}, \text{Hypozedic}\}$ the broader class the
patient’s diagnosis falls into, and T1 & T2 the two test results shown
on Screen 2. P(D) = prior probability of each candidate disease as
established by the baseline frequency chart shown on Screen 1.
$$P(T = t \mid D) = \begin{cases} 0.7 & t = D \\ 0.1 & t \ne D \end{cases}$$

$$P(D \mid T_1, T_2) = \frac{P(D)\, P(T_1 \mid D)\, P(T_2 \mid D)}{\sum_{D'} P(D')\, P(T_1 \mid D')\, P(T_2 \mid D')}$$

$$P(C = \text{Hypozedic} \mid T_1, T_2) = \sum_{D \in \{Y_1, Y_2\}} P(D \mid T_1, T_2)$$
As shown above, our baseline normative model follows standard Bayesian
updating to calculate the posterior over each of the four candidate
diseases. Following @jern2014, the likelihood of a test correctly
identifying the patient’s true disease is set to 0.7, with each of the
three possible spurious results assigned a likelihood of 0.1. Beliefs
about the broader class the patient's diagnosis falls into are obtained
by summing the posterior probability over the candidate diseases
belonging to that class.

## Model 2: Normative Model Initalized with Empirical Priors

### Formalization

Let $D \in \{L_1, L_2, Y_1, Y_2\}$ again represent the patient's true
disease, $C \in \{\text{Allozedic}, \text{Hypozedic}\}$ the broader
class the patient’s diagnosis falls into, and T1 & T2 the two test
results shown on Screen 2.

P(D) = participants' empirical priors over the four candidate diseases.
To obtain these values, we first used the following linear mixed effects
model to calculate participants’ estimated marginal beliefs across
conditions (polarization, moderation, and control) and phases (initial
and final):

```         
Rating ~ Phase × Condition + (1 | Participant)
```

We then re-scaled the baseline frequency chart proportions so that each
disease class's total matched the model's estimate at the initial phase.
Within each class, the relative proportions between the two diseases
remained fixed at those established by the baseline frequency chart. To
calculate the posterior over each of the four candidate diseases, Model
2 follows an identical Bayesian updating procedure to Model 1:

$$P(T = t \mid D) = \begin{cases} 0.7 & t = D \\ 0.1 & t \ne D \end{cases}$$

$$P(D \mid T_1, T_2) = \frac{P(D)\, P(T_1 \mid D)\, P(T_2 \mid D)}{\sum_{D'} P(D')\, P(T_1 \mid D')\, P(T_2 \mid D')}$$

$$P(C = \text{Hypozedic} \mid T_1, T_2) = \sum_{D \in \{Y_1, Y_2\}} P(D \mid T_1, T_2)$$

## Model 3: Joint Inference Model Initialized with Empirical Priors

### Formalization

As in Models 1 and 2, let D{L1,L2,Y1,Y2} represent the patient's true
disease,C{Allozedic,Hypozedic} the broader class the patient’s diagnosis
falls into, and T1 & T2 the two test results shown on Screen 2. As in
Model 2, P(D) = participants' empirical priors over the four candidate
diseases.

Building upon Models 1 and 2, let $\theta$ represent the reliability of
the tests which produced the results shown on Screen 2.

We then estimate participants' uncertainty about the true value of
$\theta$ using a discrete grid of candidate values
$\theta_1, \theta_2, \dots, \theta_n \in (0,1)$ ($n = 2000$, evenly
spaced) Each candidate value of $\theta$ is assigned a prior weight
reflecting how plausible that value is believed to be, obtained using
the following Beta distribution:

$$P(\theta_i) = \frac{\text{Beta}(\theta_i;\ 0.7\kappa,\ 0.3\kappa)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \text{Beta}(\theta_j;\ 0.7\kappa,\ 0.3\kappa)}$$
As shown above, we centered the distribution at 0.7 given that the
framing on Screen 2 (following @jern2014) implies a reliability rate of
0.7. The parameter $\kappa$ controls how concentrated participants’
priors are around the 0.7 center. Larger values of $\kappa$ represent
greater certainty in a reliability rate approximating 0.7, while smaller
$\kappa$ values represent less certainty (i.e., openness to a greater
spread of reliability rates). Before calculating the likelihood of the
observed test results given a fixed candidate value for $\theta$, we
rewrite the likelihood function from Models 1 and 2 such that:

$$P(T = t \mid D, \theta_i) = \begin{cases} \theta_i & t = D \\ \dfrac{1-\theta_i}{3} & t \ne D \end{cases}$$

We then calculate the likelihood of the observed test results at each
candidate value for $\theta$, before marginalizing across each of the
four candidate diseases:

$$P(T_1, T_2 \mid \theta_i) = \sum_{D} P(D)\, P(T_1 \mid D, \theta_i)\, P(T_2 \mid D, \theta_i)$$

Next, we use standard Bayesian updating to estimate participants’
posterior beliefs over $\theta$:

$$P(\theta_i \mid T_1, T_2) = \frac{P(\theta_i)\, P(T_1, T_2 \mid \theta_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} P(\theta_j)\, P(T_1, T_2 \mid \theta_j)}$$

This allows us to compute participants' posterior beliefs about the
patient’s diagnosis under each candidate $\theta$:

$$P(D \mid T_1, T_2, \theta_i) = \frac{P(D)\, P(T_1 \mid D, \theta_i)\, P(T_2 \mid D, \theta_i)}{\sum_{D'} P(D')\, P(T_1 \mid D', \theta_i)\, P(T_2 \mid D', \theta_i)}$$

Finally, we marginalize across all candidate $\theta$ values, weighting
each of the calculated diagnosis posteriors by its corresponding
posterior weight $P(\theta_i \mid T_1, T_2)$:

$$P(D \mid T_1, T_2) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} P(D \mid T_1, T_2, \theta_i)\, P(\theta_i \mid T_1, T_2)$$

$$P(C = \text{Hypozedic} \mid T_1, T_2) = \sum_{D \in \{Y_1, Y_2\}} P(D \mid T_1, T_2)$$

This is equivalent to treating $D$ and $\theta$ as jointly inferred from
the outset, with the joint posterior over disease and reliability
written as:

$$P(D, \theta_i \mid T_1, T_2) = \frac{P(D)\, P(\theta_i)\, P(T_1 \mid D, \theta_i)\, P(T_2 \mid D, \theta_i)}{\sum_{D'} \sum_{j} P(D')\, P(\theta_j)\, P(T_1 \mid D', \theta_j)\, P(T_2 \mid D', \theta_j)}$$

and the posterior over the disease is obtained by marginalizing over all
candidate values of $\theta$ as:

$$P(D \mid T_1, T_2) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} P(D \mid T_1, T_2, \theta_i)\, P(\theta_i \mid T_1, T_2)$$

If we substitute the expressions for $P(D \mid T_1, T_2, \theta_i)$ and
$P(\theta_i \mid T_1, T_2)$ into this posterior:

$$P(D \mid T_1, T_2) = \sum_i \frac{P(D)\, P(T_1 \mid D, \theta_i)\, P(T_2 \mid D, \theta_i)}{P(T_1, T_2 \mid \theta_i)} \cdot \frac{P(\theta_i)\, P(T_1, T_2 \mid \theta_i)}{\sum_j P(\theta_j)\, P(T_1, T_2 \mid \theta_j)}$$

The $P(T_1, T_2 \mid \theta_i)$ term cancels out, giving us:

$$P(D \mid T_1, T_2) = \frac{\sum_i P(D)\, P(\theta_i)\, P(T_1 \mid D, \theta_i)\, P(T_2 \mid D, \theta_i)}{\sum_j P(\theta_j)\, P(T_1, T_2 \mid \theta_j)}$$

which is the the joint posterior $P(D, \theta_i \mid T_1, T_2)$.

## Model 4: Joint Inference Model Initialized with Uniform Prior Over Theta

**Formalization**

Following Model 3, let $\theta$ represent the reliability of the tests
which produced the results shown on Screen 2.

We then estimate participants' uncertainty about the true value of
$\theta$ using a discrete grid of candidate values
$\theta_1, \theta_2, \dots, \theta_n \in (0,1)$ ($n = 2000$, evenly
spaced) Each candidate value of $\theta$ is assigned a prior weight
reflecting how plausible that value is believed to be, obtained using
the following Beta distribution:

$$P(\theta_i) = \frac{\text{Beta}(\theta_i;\ 1,\ 1)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \text{Beta}(\theta_j;\ 1,\ 1)}$$
As shown above, Model 4 diverges from Model 3 in that we no longer
center the distribution at 0.7. We chose to incorporate a uniform
distribution of priors over theta to reflect total uncertainty about the
tests' reliability, given participants were not provided with a
reliability rate.

From here, Model 4's computations are identical to those outlined in the
formalization for Model 3 above.
